I was an assistant junior high school teacher, and was outside helping the PE teacher set up for the upcoming sports festival. His statement caught me off guard, because I knew I'd been using the "male" pronoun 僕. I wasn't yet aware of any other features of gendered language in Japanese, so I assumed it had something to do with my intonation — usually a dead giveaway that I'm gay when speaking English. 「どんなところが女の子っぽいですか。」"In what way is it girly?" I asked. 「いつも『〜わ』って言ってるところとか。」"Maybe the way you're always ending sentences with 〜わ." This answer only confused me further, because I had definitely heard men more masculine than I stick 〜わ to the end of their sentences too. It made me wonder what other aspects of my language use were communicating information I wasn't aware of. Over time, I came to understand that Japanese is full of different language features that communicate your gender identity. In English, we rely on others to call us by our preferred pronouns, such as "he," "she," or "they," but in Japanese, the power to express your gender through language often rests in your hands. As great as this is, the array of gendered language choices can be hard to navigate, and many language learners receive overly-simplified or contradictory advice about gendered language use. Even if you identify as cisgender (a person whose gender identity and birth sex are the same), the traditional "girls use this, boys use that" explanation for gendered Japanese can be hard to wrap your mind around. If you don't identify that way, it's even more difficult to figure out! This article aims to give a more queer-inclusive overview of gendered Japanese language use. We'll take a look at the stereotypical gendered language speech styles known as 女言葉 ("women's language") and 男言葉 ("men's language"), and then dive deeper into how speakers deviate from these linguistic gender norms in real life. We'll also discuss オネエ言葉, another stereotypical gendered language style that originated in the gay bar scene, and is now highly visible in Japanese media. fetched_contents.text: TW Queer Japan: Towards Gender Freedom in Japanese Language In contrast to many Indo-European (including Romance, Slavic and Germanic) languages, Japanese has no grammatical gender in its nouns or adjective agreement. Moreover, the Japanese honorifics such as -san and -sama are gender-neutral, which contrasts with Mr., Ms. or Mx. titles in English. However, Japanese is still a deeply gendered language. As Cameron Lombardo writes in his article “Beyond the Binary: A Queer Take on Gendered Japanese,” the extreme ends of the gendered speech style spectrum in Japanese are represented by women’s language (onna kotoba) and men’s language (otoko kotoba). Stereotypically feminine and masculine styles of spoken Japanese are differentiated by their inflections — the upward tones of the feminine and the deeper, descending tones of the masculine — choice of nouns and slang, their ending particles (-wa versus -da), and the “I,” the ever-present choice of the personal pronoun. The most common first-person pronouns, from stereotypically feminine to stereotypically masculine, are: atashi, watashi, jibun, boku and ore. But there are many instances of moving away from stereotypes and subverting gendered language in Japan. Photo by Mark X. Farmer Girl Group Idols and Boyish Pronouns Many people have noted that gender neutrality appears in surprising places in Japan. Notably, idol culture and the use of boku, the boyish “I” in song lyrics. In songs like “Polyrhythm” by Perfume or “Everyday, Katyusha” by AKB48, the singers often refer to themselves as boku. Given the hyper-feminization and patriarchal underpinnings of the female idol industry, it’s difficult to suggest that these groups or their lyricists are intending to subvert the gender binary. Rather, writers like Takaya Ohta and Kazuto Matsumiya suggest that this use of boku subconsciously separates the singers from the characters they play in their songs. This separation between singer and character serves several functions. It creates a neutral love song men and women can easily empathize with and avoids controversy or backlash over lyrics. It also protects the illusion that the idol is not singing about her personal relationship and is therefore still available. Matsumiya further speculates that the pairing of boku and kimi uses fewer syllables and is easier to write into lyrics than the longer watashi or anata. “Watashi or kimi would make the song sound like it’s about a boss and a subordinate,” he points out. Editorial credit: Morumotto / Shutterstock.com Onee Kotoba And Queer-Coded Language Queer groups and their diverse gender and sexual identities have subverted language throughout recorded history and Japan is no exception. Lesbian communities have used masculine pronouns and gay men sometimes use atypically feminine pronouns like atashi. Popularized by queer television talents, onee kotoba (literally “older sister speak”) is the dialect of Japanese most often associated with the LGBTQ community, often involving flamboyant mannerisms, over-the-top feminine speech and vulgar slang. Not unlike the highly stylized dialect used by drag queens on RuPaul’s Drag Race (which has its roots in queer African American Vernacular English), onee kotoba walks a fine line for many Japanese people. ## Media-linguistics evidence on pronouns, sentence-end particles, and media shaping language

The broader media-linguistics literature in the evidence supports the idea that **media and social environments can shape language use**, especially around **pronouns** and **sentence-end particles**. The strongest evidence is from **social media**, where studies examine linguistic simplification, complexity over time, and the role of first-person pronouns and emotional interjections in interaction [N1-R1][N1-R5]. It also shows that social media language affects interaction and communication [N1-R3]. This suggests that media exposure can influence **speech style and written style**, at least in digital interaction contexts [N1-R1][N1-R3].

On **pronouns**, the evidence is especially clear that pronouns can be **socially marked** and tied to **norm conflict**. One paper explicitly studies how norm conflict is talked about with regard to standard language and regional varieties in touristic settings, showing that pronouns can signal alignment or conflict with social norms [N1-R2]. Another study is about a **sociolinguistic study of generic pronouns**, indicating that pronouns can be treated as socially marked and used to express generalized reference [N1-R4]. These sources support the broader claim that pronouns are socially marked and can be shaped by media or social environments, even if the specific Japanese evidence is thin [N1-R2][N1-R4].

On **sentence-end particles**, the evidence is more descriptive than causal. The Japanese-language sources explain that sentence-ending particles such as *ne*, *yo*, *na*, and *zo* are small but **emotionally and relationally significant** features in Japanese, adding tone, attitude, and relational meaning rather than simply conveying logic [N4-F4]. They are described as optional grammatically but essential for natural speech, since dropping them makes speech sound robotic [N4-F4]. The sources also note that *wa* is often associated with **feminine assertion and emotional expression**, while *na* is traditionally considered **masculine self-reflection or emotional expression**, and that usage patterns can vary by speaker and context [N4-F4]. This shows that sentence-end particles are treated as **socially marked categories** in Japanese: they are not neutral, but are tied to **gendered tone**, **relationality**, and **emotional nuance** [N4-F4][N4-R4].

The evidence also supports the idea that **media exposure can influence speech or written style**. The social media studies show that users’ comments and interaction patterns change over time and that emotional interjections and first-person pronouns are frequent in social media language [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Another study on social media language explicitly examines how **language on social media platforms** affects interaction and communication, reinforcing the plausibility that media exposure can shape expressive style [N1-R3]. The broader media-linguistics literature in the evidence therefore suggests that **media environments can shape both the form and the function** of speech, especially in ways that are visible in pronouns, particles, and interactional style [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

## What the evidence does *not* show clearly

Importantly, the supplied evidence does **not** provide direct Japanese-language studies proving a causal link between **specific media exposure** and **pronoun use or sentence-end particles** in the way the user asks. It does, however, support the general claim that **media and social environments can shape language use**, especially in the areas of **pronouns** and **sentence-ending particles** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N4-F4]. So the safest conclusion is: **yes, the broader literature suggests media can influence language, but the Japanese-specific causal evidence in these materials is limited** [N1-R1][N1-R3][N4-F4].
